paragraphs: What we have just said confirms Chapter XVI and makes it clear that instituting government is not a contract but a law. Those who hold the executive power are not the people’s masters but its officers. The people can appoint them and dismiss them whenever it pleases. For them the question is never one of contract, only of obedience. When they take on the functions the State imposes on them, they are merely doing their duty as citizens, and they have no right at all to argue over the terms.

So when the people sets up a hereditary government, whether a monarchy limited to one family or an aristocracy limited to one class, it is not taking on an obligation. It is giving the administration a provisional form, which stands until the people decides to order it differently.

It is true that such changes are always dangerous, and that an established government should never be disturbed unless it becomes incompatible with the public good. But this caution is a maxim of policy, not a rule of right. The State is no more obliged to leave civil authority with its rulers than to leave military authority with its generals.

It is also true that one cannot be too careful, in such cases, to observe every formality needed to tell a regular, legitimate act apart from a seditious tumult, and the will of a whole people from the clamor of a faction. Here above all, one should grant the unwelcome possibility no more than strict logic forces one to grant. Yet the prince gains a great advantage from this requirement: he can hold on to his power against the people without anyone being able to say he has usurped it. Since he appears to be using only his rights, he easily extends them. Under the pretext of keeping the peace, he prevents the assemblies meant to restore order. He exploits a silence he refuses to let anyone break, and irregularities he causes himself, to presume the backing of those whom fear keeps from speaking, and to punish those who dare to speak. This is how the decemvirs, elected first for one year and then kept in office for a second, tried to make their power permanent by forbidding the comitia to assemble. By this easy method every government in the world, once clothed with public power, sooner or later usurps the sovereign authority.

The periodic assemblies I have already described are meant to prevent or delay this calamity, above all when no formal summons is needed. Then the prince cannot stop them without openly declaring himself a lawbreaker and an enemy of the State.
These assemblies have the sole purpose of maintaining the social compact. They should always open by putting two propositions that cannot be suppressed and that are voted on separately.
The first is: “Is it the Sovereign’s pleasure to keep the present form of government?”
The second is: “Is it the people’s pleasure that those who now hold the administration should keep it?”

Here I am taking for granted what I believe I have shown: the State has no fundamental law that cannot be revoked, not even the social compact itself. If all the citizens assembled and agreed to break the compact, there is no doubt it would be broken quite legitimately. Grotius even holds that each man can renounce his membership in his own State and, on leaving the country, take back his natural liberty and his goods.[1] It would be absurd if all the citizens assembled could not do what each of them can do alone.
